name: Cold laser scalp device

lead: A cold laser scalp device shines low-power red or near-infrared light on the scalp, in the form of a cap, comb or helmet. People use it to increase hair density and slow thinning from androgenetic alopecia.

Wikipedia reports that low-level laser therapy has been shown to increase hair density and growth in both sexes, with a 2017 review finding that 10 of 11 trials showed significant improvement. Earlier reviews were mixed and larger long-term blinded trials are called for.

paras: Users wear or pass the device over the scalp for short sessions several times a week, often alongside other hair treatments. Wikipedia reports that device type and treatment duration did not appear to change effectiveness.
Side effects are generally described as mild. Several laser devices are FDA-cleared, and the FDA has acted against firms making broad disease claims for such devices, so product status varies.

angle.text: Users apply the light to thinning areas to increase hair density. Studies report improvement versus baseline in most trials, with ongoing use typically described as necessary.

lead: Low-level laser therapy (also called cold laser therapy or photobiomodulation) applies low-power lasers or LEDs to the skin. For hair, it is delivered through caps, combs or helmets aimed at the scalp [1].

Proponents use it to increase hair density and slow thinning. The accepted theory centers on a mitochondrial enzyme, cytochrome c oxidase, though effectiveness is described as still under investigation [1]. Wikipedia says red and infrared light work better for androgenetic alopecia [1].

A 2017 review found 10 of 11 trials improved versus baseline or controls, whereas 2012 to 2015 reviews ranged from little evidence to tentative benefit; some reviewers suggest it may match minoxidil or finasteride but call for larger blinded long-term trials [1].

paras: The commonly cited explanation involves cytochrome c oxidase in mitochondria absorbing light, but effects appear limited to certain wavelengths and the mechanism is still being studied [1].

Wikipedia reports that LLLT increased hair density and growth in men and women, and that device type (hat, comb, helmet) did not appear to alter results [1]. Reviews differ in strength, and some suggest comparability with drug treatments pending larger trials [1].
Several LLLT devices are FDA-cleared, and in 2015 the FDA obtained a permanent injunction against QLaser PMA for marketing devices for over 200 diseases [1].
A 2017 review cited by Wikipedia found significant improvement in 10 of 11 trials for androgenetic alopecia; earlier reviews were less certain [1].
